summary.text: A 2-year-old boy came to the Department of Oral Mucosa clinic after his parents complained of whitening of the buccal mucosa for 1 year. He had no obvious symptoms. Examination showed large creamy white folds of uneven thickness on the buccal mucosa, with flaking mucosa that could be swabbed off without bleeding or erosion, and no lesions of the tongue or mouth floor. His father and twin sisters exhibited similar oral lesions.

The authors report white sponge nevus in four members of the family, including the proband. Peripheral venous blood from the proband and both parents underwent trio whole-exome sequencing with paternal Sanger validation. The proband carried a heterozygous deletion in exon 1 of the K4 gene, an aspartic acid loss, and no abnormality was found in his mother. Table 1 lists 4 of 5 family members as affected.

One week later, the outpatient review showed that the lesion area of the bilateral buccal mucosa was significantly reduced and the white corrugated plaques basically disappeared. Three months later, the bilateral buccal mucosa redeveloped grayish white corrugated folds and plaques (Figure 8).

summary.text: The proband’s father had white lesions of the buccal mucosa on both sides, described as large gray and white folds and plaques, spongy and painless. He had no obvious symptoms in his oral mucosa, had never consulted a doctor and had not received any treatment before this incident.

Because the proband was young, a histological examination was done on the father’s intraoral lesion with his informed consent. It showed incompletely keratinized surface cells, enlarged vacuolated edematous spiny cells with nuclear pyknosis, well-differentiated basal cells and no inflammatory infiltration, and WSN was confirmed. Sequencing found a heterozygous K4 exon 1 deletion, an aspartic acid loss.

He was treated with topical retinoic acid cream three times a day. One week later the bilateral buccal lesion area was significantly reduced and the white corrugated plaques had basically disappeared. After three months the bilateral buccal mucosa again showed grayish white corrugated folds and plaques, which the authors state verified recurrence of WSN.

summary.text: A twin sister of the proband, one of the monozygotic twins, had oral lesions since birth in the same areas as her brother and father but with thicker folds. Large white corrugated folds resembling a sponge involved the right and left buccal mucosa and the inner mucosa of the upper lip, and the plaques were painless.

The authors state that WSN was confirmed in the monozygotic twins. Genetic sequencing was not performed for the twin sisters because they were only six months old, and no biopsy or treatment is described for her.
